articles.title: LIVE: GMP student officer arrested on suspicion of rape and kidnap after M62 pursuit
articles.excerpt: LIVE updates after a 23-year-old Greater Manchester Police student officer was arrested on suspicion of rape, kidnap and dangerous driving following a pursuit on the M62.
articles.content_html:
LIVE UPDATES — This story is being updated as further confirmed information becomes available.

18:50 — Greater Manchester Police says it is committed to working with the Crown Prosecution Service to bring the case to court as quickly as possible, while also accelerating misconduct proceedings within police regulations. Assistant Chief Constable Mark Dexter said the allegations were deeply concerning and disturbing and said all necessary and decisive action would be taken in the interests of the woman and the public.

GMP has confirmed its Professional Standards Directorate carried out an initial review of the officer's vetting and found it had been completed without any reason for concern. The force stressed that this did not lessen the severity of the allegations.

18:42 — Rochdale Daily moved this breaking story to live coverage. We will add confirmed developments from Greater Manchester Police, the Independent Office for Police Conduct and other authoritative sources as they emerge.

WHAT WE KNOW SO FAR

A 23-year-old Greater Manchester Police student officer has been arrested on suspicion of rape and kidnap following a police pursuit on the M62.

The officer was off duty when a 999 call was received shortly before 10.20pm on Saturday. Police said a woman in her 20s could be heard in distress in a vehicle in the Manchester area.

Officers traced the suspect's personal vehicle and began a pursuit. The pursuit continued onto the M62 before the officer was detained in West Yorkshire.

The 23-year-old was arrested on suspicion of rape, kidnap and dangerous driving. GMP says he has been suspended from duty and remains in custody for questioning.

The woman is being supported by specialist officers and other agencies.

Greater Manchester Police has made a voluntary referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct. Internal misconduct proceedings are also being progressed.

Assistant Chief Constable Mark Dexter said thousands of GMP officers and staff who work to protect the public would be shocked and angered by the allegations. He said specialist resources had been assigned to the investigation and gave a commitment that the force would work with prosecutors as the criminal investigation progresses.

The allegations have not been proven. An arrest does not amount to a finding of guilt and the officer is entitled to the presumption of innocence unless and until convicted. This live page will be updated when further information is confirmed.

articles.title: Edenfield Road reopens early after resurfacing work completed ahead of schedule
articles.excerpt: Edenfield Road between the White Lion and Nutters has reopened early after contractors completed resurfacing and lining work ahead of schedule.
articles.content_html:
Edenfield Road between the White Lion and Nutters has reopened to traffic after resurfacing works were completed ahead of schedule.

Norden councillor Paul Ellison MBE confirmed on Saturday that the road is now open and that the road closure which had been expected on Sunday will no longer be required.

Contractors completed the main resurfacing work early, with Saturday seeing the final road-lining work carried out. Cat's-eye road studs are due to be fitted on Monday, but the road itself has reopened.

Councillor Ellison thanked Rochdale Borough Council, A&T Surfacing and Rhodes & Son Construction for completing the scheme ahead of schedule, describing the finished work as a fantastic job.

The reopening will be welcome news for residents and motorists using one of the principal routes through Norden. The works had required traffic restrictions while the carriageway was resurfaced, with further closure time originally expected over the weekend.

With the contractors finishing earlier than planned, drivers can now use the stretch between the White Lion and Nutters without the anticipated Sunday closure.

Motorists should remain aware that the final cat's-eye inserts are expected to be fitted on Monday and should follow any temporary traffic management in place while that work is completed.

articles.title: New Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig visits Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Newly elected Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig is visiting Rochdale today as she begins work across the city-region following her victory in last month's mayoral by-election.
articles.content_html:
Newly elected Mayor of Greater Manchester Bev Craig is visiting Rochdale today, bringing the new city-region mayor to the borough during the opening days of her term.

Craig was elected at the Greater Manchester mayoral by-election on 30 July, succeeding Andy Burnham after his return to Westminster. She became the first woman to hold the Greater Manchester mayoralty.

The visit puts Rochdale among the places receiving early attention from the new mayor as she begins the job of representing all ten Greater Manchester boroughs.

At the time of publication, no detailed public itinerary or standalone press release about today's Rochdale visit had been published on the Greater Manchester Combined Authority news pages. Rochdale Daily has checked publicly available material from the mayoral and GMCA press operation and will update this article if further details, photographs or statements are released.

Craig arrives in Rochdale having campaigned on a platform that included expanding the Bee Network, freezing bus fares and extending free bus travel to young people aged 11 to 18. She has also placed housing, economic growth and reducing inequalities among the central issues facing Greater Manchester.

Those priorities are particularly relevant to Rochdale, where transport connectivity, town-centre investment, housing and access to opportunity remain major local issues.

Before becoming mayor, Craig led Manchester City Council from December 2021 and held Greater Manchester responsibilities for economy, business and inclusive growth. She was awarded an OBE in March 2026 for services to local government.

Her election followed the departure of Andy Burnham from the mayoralty. Craig won the contest after the count proceeded to a second round, defeating Reform UK's Sian Astley.

Today's Rochdale visit will therefore be watched for signs of how the new mayor intends to translate her city-region promises into action for individual boroughs outside Manchester city centre.

Rochdale Daily will add any confirmed detail released by the mayor's press team about the purpose of the visit, people she met or commitments made while in the borough.

articles.title: Councillor Daniel Meredith backs stronger Hornets partnership after Superhero Day
articles.excerpt: Balderstone and Kirkholt councillor Daniel Meredith has praised Rochdale Hornets' Superhero Day and highlighted talks about how the club and council can work together to strengthen rugby and community spirit across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Balderstone and Kirkholt councillor Daniel Meredith has praised Rochdale Hornets' Superhero Day after spending the afternoon at the club's council-sponsored fixture with his family.

Meredith attended the Hornets men's match against Whitehaven, although the afternoon produced mixed fortunes for Rochdale's teams.

The men's side narrowly lost to Whitehaven, while the Hornets women recorded a victory against Leigh Miners. Meredith joked that he may have been the day's 'jinx', having watched the men's defeat but missed the women's win while his daughter Meadhbh was having her afternoon nap.

Despite the result, Meredith described it as a great afternoon and said the council-sponsored match provided an opportunity to discuss the relationship between Rochdale Hornets and Rochdale Borough Council.

He said it was 'brilliant' to be at the game and to speak about how the Hornets and the council can continue working together to strengthen both rugby and community spirit across Rochdale.

The comments underline the wider community role played by Rochdale Hornets beyond results on the pitch, with the club's men's and women's teams, family matchdays and community activity providing opportunities to bring residents together around the sport.

Superhero Day added a family-focused theme to the fixture, encouraging supporters of different ages to take part in the matchday experience.

Meredith is a Labour and Co-operative councillor representing Balderstone and Kirkholt and serves as Rochdale Borough Council's cabinet member for regeneration and housing.

The men's result may not have gone Rochdale's way, but Meredith's message after the afternoon was focused firmly on the future: building on cooperation between the council and Hornets to support rugby and community life across the borough.

articles.title: £12m plan aims to bring Storage World Middleton site back to life after devastating fire
articles.excerpt: A £12m rebirth bid has been launched for the Storage World site in Middleton, more than a year after a devastating fire destroyed the Old Hall Street facility.
articles.content_html:
A £12m bid to bring the Storage World site in Middleton back to life has been launched, marking a major potential investment in an important part of the town centre following last year's devastating fire.

The proposals concern the Storage World site on Old Hall Street, next to Middleton Arena. The former storage facility was badly damaged by a major blaze in June 2025, which burned for several days and led to demolition of the building. No injuries were reported, although customers and businesses suffered significant losses.

Place North West has reported that Storage World has now launched a £12m rebirth bid for the site. The move comes as regeneration work and planning for the wider Middleton town centre area continues.

Official Rochdale Development Agency updates show that the council and RDA have remained in discussions with Storage World since the fire. In June, the RDA said it was working with stakeholders to develop key principles for the area, including the potential to deliver improvements to Middleton Arena and create a new public space. It also confirmed that discussions with Storage World were continuing with input from Rochdale Borough Council's planning team.

The site is particularly significant because of its position beside Middleton Arena and within an area being considered as part of wider plans for the future of Middleton town centre. Earlier council reports said the outcomes of discussions over Storage World and the arena would feed into wider masterplanning work.

Before the fire, Storage World operated a large self-storage and workspace facility from Old Hall Street. The Middleton operation had previously expanded as demand grew, with the company providing traditional storage alongside space used by small and online businesses.

The 2025 blaze had a substantial impact on customers. Fire crews worked for days at the scene and parts of the building were demolished while firefighting operations were still under way to allow crews safe access. Storage World said at the time that its team was devastated by the impact on customers and the wider community.

The latest £12m proposal therefore represents a potentially significant next chapter for a prominent town-centre site and comes at a time when Middleton is the subject of wider regeneration and masterplanning proposals.

Rochdale Daily will update this story as further planning documents and details of the proposed redevelopment become publicly available.

articles.title: Police promise increased patrols around The Strand after resident reports verbal abuse
articles.excerpt: Police say they will speak to two shops and increase patrols around The Strand and Kirkway after a resident reported being verbally abused by a man who had been begging in the area.
articles.content_html:
Police have told a Kirkholt resident that patrols will be increased around The Strand and Kirkway following a reported incident involving a man begging and verbally abusing her last week.

The resident said she received a positive telephone call from police on Monday afternoon after reporting the incident at The Strand.

According to the resident, officers said they intend to speak to staff at two shops in the area as part of efforts to identify the man involved. If he can be identified, police indicated that appropriate action would be considered.

The resident said officers also told her that police are taking this type of behaviour seriously and intend to increase patrols around The Strand and Kirkway.

The response will be welcomed by residents and businesses concerned about antisocial behaviour in the area. The Strand is an important neighbourhood hub used by families, shoppers and people accessing local community facilities, and residents should be able to use the area without feeling intimidated or being subjected to abuse.

Begging itself and antisocial or abusive behaviour are not necessarily the same thing, and people experiencing homelessness or financial hardship should not automatically be treated as offenders. However, threatening, intimidating or verbally abusive behaviour can be reported to police, particularly where somebody feels unsafe.

The reported incident remains an allegation and Rochdale Daily is not identifying the man involved. No suggestion is made that he has committed a criminal offence unless and until police establish the circumstances and take any appropriate action.

Anyone experiencing threatening or abusive behaviour can report it to Greater Manchester Police. Where there is an immediate danger or a crime is in progress, residents should call 999.

articles.title: Videos raise hygiene concerns at one-star Halifax Road halal meat shop
articles.excerpt: Videos circulating on social media have prompted questions about food hygiene at Rajdhani Halal Meats on Halifax Road, which is listed with a one-star food hygiene rating.
articles.content_html:
Videos circulating on social media have prompted fresh questions about food hygiene at Rajdhani Halal Meats, 115 Halifax Road, Rochdale, after footage was shared which appears to show meat being handled outside close to commercial waste bins.

The footage has been discussed on local social-media groups, where residents have called for the circumstances to be investigated. Screenshots accompanying the posts show a person working behind the premises near large bins and commercial equipment. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified when the footage was recorded, exactly what type of meat was being handled, or whether the activity shown breached food-safety regulations.

Separate published food-hygiene information lists Rajdhani Halal Meats with a food hygiene rating of 1 — 'major improvement necessary' — following an inspection recorded on 25 June 2025.

A one-star food hygiene rating does not in itself establish that food currently being sold by a business is unsafe. It records the assessment made by inspectors at the time of the relevant inspection and businesses can make improvements or seek reassessment.

The circulating footage is nevertheless likely to prompt questions about whether further investigation or inspection is required. Food businesses are required to follow hygiene controls designed to protect food from contamination during storage, preparation and handling.

Residents concerned about food hygiene at a premises can report their concerns to the relevant local authority environmental-health service.

Rochdale Daily is inviting Rajdhani Halal Meats to explain the circumstances shown in the footage, including when it was recorded, what activity was taking place and whether any subsequent changes have been made.

The business is also invited to provide evidence of any more recent inspection or updated food-hygiene assessment. Any substantive response will be added prominently to this article.

articles.content_html:
The Summit Inn has reopened its doors with a new menu packed with traditional pub favourites, homemade dishes and lighter lunch options.

The refreshed offering includes starters and light bites from £6, with homemade soup of the day served with bread and butter. Other starters include a black pudding stack with potato cake, poached egg and English mustard sauce for £8.50; chicken liver pâté with cranberry sauce and toast for £8; garlic mushrooms on toasted sourdough for £8.50; lamb koftas with roasted red pepper houmous and pitta for £8.50; traditional prawn cocktail for £8.50; Cajun chicken skewers for £7.50; and chicken tenders for £7.95.

A selection of cold sandwiches is priced at £7, served on white or brown bloomer with a dressed salad garnish. Fillings include roast ham and English mustard, roast beef and horseradish, roast turkey and stuffing, tuna mayonnaise, and savoury cheese and onion. Diners can add a small bowl of homemade soup for £4 or homemade chips or skinny fries for £3.

The hot sandwich menu includes a classic BLT for £11, while a braised steak sandwich with slow-cooked beef, onion gravy and fries is £13. A triple-decker chicken and bacon club and a tuna melt are also £13, with toasted home-cooked ham and cheddar or cheddar and tomato sandwiches priced at £12.

For those looking for something lighter, salads include a £12.95 Ploughman's Lunch with homemade pâté, cheese, home-cooked ham, mixed salad, apple, celery, onion chutney and crusty bread. Chicken and bacon salad, chicken Caesar salad and halloumi salad are also available at £12.95.

The new menu combines familiar pub dishes with several homemade elements and gives customers options ranging from a bowl of soup or sandwich through to a more substantial lunch.

The reopening brings another food option back into service for residents and visitors, with the Summit Inn welcoming customers to try the new menu.

articles.title: This week in Rochdale, 100 years ago: the town captured from the air in August 1926
articles.excerpt: Exactly a century ago this month, aerial photographers captured remarkable views of Rochdale's Town Hall, Yorkshire Street, railway station, Broadfield Park and industrial works — preserving the town as it looked in August 1926.
articles.content_html:
One hundred years ago this week, Rochdale was a very different town — but thanks to a remarkable series of aerial photographs taken in August 1926, we can still see it almost street by street.

The images, held by the Britain From Above archive, show a dense industrial town of mills, railway infrastructure, tramways, terraced streets and civic buildings. They provide one of the clearest surviving visual records of Rochdale in the inter-war period.

Yorkshire Street was photographed from the air in August 1926 under reference EPW016788. The view shows the familiar line of the street threading through tightly packed buildings, with factories, chimneys and terraced housing occupying much of the surrounding landscape. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016788

Rochdale railway station was also captured that month under reference EPW016784. The photograph shows not only the station but the extraordinary concentration of railway sidings, engineering works and industrial premises that once surrounded this part of the town. The archive identifies features including railway works, cotton mills, a goods shed and the Rochdale Canal terminal basin. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016784

Another image, EPW016791, looks across Town Hall Square. It records landmarks that remain instantly recognisable alongside features which have since vanished or changed beyond recognition. Archive annotations identify St Chad's, the Esplanade, Rochdale Post Office, Drake Street, tramcars and the Rochdale War Memorial while it was still under construction. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016791

Broadfield Park was photographed in the same month under reference EPW016782, giving another extraordinary perspective across the civic heart of Rochdale. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016782

The industrial scale of the town is perhaps most obvious in the August 1926 photographs of Fishwick Street. Image EPW016789 records the railway works there, reflecting the huge engineering and manufacturing presence which once surrounded Rochdale's rail network. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016789

Even before that August series, an Aerofilms photograph taken on 6 August 1926 captured Rochdale Road crossing the railway and Rochdale Canal at Slattocks. The image, EPW016440, preserves a landscape where canal, railway and road infrastructure sat side by side — the transport arteries which helped power the borough's industrial economy. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016440

What is striking about these photographs is not simply what has disappeared. It is how much remains legible. The Town Hall, St Chad's, major road alignments and parts of the railway landscape allow modern residents to orient themselves inside a town photographed from an aircraft a century ago.

The photographs also capture Rochdale during a period of profound change. The borough remained heavily industrial, public transport still included corporation tramcars, and mills and engineering works dominated huge areas which today contain housing, roads, offices and redeveloped land.

The Rochdale Observer itself was already a long-established part of town life by 1926, having first appeared in 1856. Its surviving archive means future editions of Rochdale Daily's '100 Years Ago' feature can go beyond photographs and recover the stories residents were actually reading — crime reports, council debates, sport, advertisements, court cases, births, deaths and the everyday incidents which made up life in the borough.

For this first edition, though, the photographs tell their own story. They allow us to look down on Rochdale exactly a century ago and recognise both the town we inherited and the one that disappeared.

Rochdale Daily intends to make 'This Week in Rochdale — 100 Years Ago' a recurring history feature throughout the centenary year.

articles.title: Inside abandoned Simpson Clough Paper Mill — and why urban exploration carries serious risks
articles.excerpt: A YouTube video has taken viewers inside the abandoned Simpson Clough Paper Mill near Rochdale, revealing remnants of its industrial past while highlighting the fascination — and dangers — of urban exploration.
articles.content_html:
An abandoned paper mill near Rochdale where machinery, equipment and remnants of its working life appear to have been left behind has been documented by urban explorers.

Footage titled 'We Found The ABANDONED Simpson Clough Paper Mill Hidden In Rochdale With Everything Left Behind!' takes viewers inside Simpson Clough Mill, offering a glimpse into an industrial site normally hidden from public view.

Watch the exploration: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pCnxD574cB8

The mill has a long industrial history. Local historical records describe Simpson Clough Mills as beginning as a fulling mill in the 1840s before being purchased by Cromptons in 1939, used for food storage during the Second World War and converted to paper manufacture after the war. The site later operated as Union Papertech and closed in January 2023.

The footage captures much of what has made so-called urban exploration, or urbex, enormously popular online. Instead of seeing industrial history restored and labelled inside a museum, viewers see workplaces in their abandoned state: machinery, offices, workshops and the gradual effects of time and nature.

For a borough whose identity was profoundly shaped by mills, manufacturing and the Industrial Revolution, sites such as Simpson Clough have an obvious historical fascination. They can provide a visual record of workplaces where generations of people spent their working lives.

But urban exploration has another side which should not be overlooked. Abandoned industrial buildings can be extremely dangerous. Water penetration, corrosion, structural deterioration and years without routine maintenance can leave floors, roofs and staircases unsafe. Broken glass, exposed metal, electrical hazards, contaminated water and hazardous materials can create further risks.

Someone injured deep inside a large former industrial complex may also be difficult for emergency services to locate and rescue.

The legal position is more complicated than saying that entering every abandoned building automatically amounts to a criminal offence. Ordinary trespass in England and Wales is generally a civil matter, but abandoned buildings and the land surrounding them still have owners. Entering private property without permission can amount to trespass, while damaging fences, doors or windows, taking property, or entering certain protected sites can raise separate criminal issues.

Rochdale Daily does not know whether the people responsible for the Simpson Clough footage had permission to enter the site and makes no allegation that any offence was committed.

The fascination with urbex is nevertheless understandable. There is something extraordinary about seeing a workplace after the workers have gone. Desks, machinery and ordinary objects can become accidental historical artefacts, and videos produced by explorers have created an informal online record of parts of Britain's disappearing industrial landscape.

The challenge is preserving that history without people putting themselves in danger or entering places unlawfully. Property owners can grant controlled access to photographers, historians and filmmakers, while heritage organisations can document industrial buildings before redevelopment or demolition.

That could be particularly valuable around Rochdale, Heywood and the surrounding valleys, where surviving industrial sites tell an important part of the borough's story.

Simpson Clough is another reminder that extraordinary pieces of local industrial history can sit quietly behind walls and fences long after their original purpose has disappeared. They are fascinating to see — but no photograph or video is worth serious injury to obtain.

Rochdale Daily does not encourage entry onto private, abandoned or restricted property without permission. Anyone wishing to document a disused site should seek the landowner's permission and follow appropriate safety requirements.

articles.title: Watching Wednesday's solar eclipse? The glasses you need to protect your eyes
articles.excerpt: Rochdale is preparing for Wednesday's major partial solar eclipse - but ordinary sunglasses are not safe. Here's what to look for in eclipse glasses and how to watch safely.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale is preparing for one of the most spectacular astronomical events visible from Britain in years, with a major partial solar eclipse due to darken the skies on Wednesday 12 August.

But anyone planning to look up needs to get one thing sorted before Wednesday evening: ordinary sunglasses are not safe for watching a solar eclipse.

Specialist solar-eclipse glasses are designed to reduce the Sun's radiation to a level suitable for direct viewing. The important marking to look for is ISO 12312-2, the international safety standard covering filters used for direct observation of the Sun.

The Royal Observatory Greenwich advises eclipse watchers to use purpose-made solar viewing protection. Eclipse glasses should be inspected before use and should not be used if the filter is scratched, torn, punctured or otherwise damaged.

WHAT SHOULD YOU BUY?

Rochdale Daily has found Astral Solar Eclipse Paper Glasses from Absolute Eclipse, designed specifically for direct solar viewing. The retailer states that the glasses comply with EN ISO 12312-2:2015 and use specialist solar-filter material.

Single pairs are advertised at approximately £4.30 based on the retailer's euro price and current exchange rates, although the exact sterling amount charged may vary with the exchange rate and payment provider. Multipacks are also available for families and groups.

BUY ASTRAL SOLAR ECLIPSE GLASSES: https://absoluteeclipse.eu/products/astral-solar-eclipse-paper-glasses?sca_ref=12037834.ocoapNfFOz&sca_source=Rochdaledaily

Rochdale Daily may receive a commission if readers purchase through the link above. This does not increase the price paid by the customer.

WHY AREN'T SUNGLASSES ENOUGH?

Even extremely dark conventional sunglasses are designed for everyday daylight, not staring directly at the Sun. During an eclipse, the reduction in visible daylight can also create a false sense that looking towards the Sun has become safer. It has not.

Looking directly at the Sun without appropriate protection can damage the retina at the back of the eye. Crucially, retinal injury may occur without immediate pain, meaning somebody may not realise damage has occurred while they are watching.

Purpose-made eclipse glasses meeting the appropriate solar-viewing standard or an indirect viewing method such as a pinhole projector should therefore be used.

CHECK YOUR GLASSES BEFORE PUTTING THEM ON

Before Wednesday's eclipse, check the solar-filter material carefully. If you find scratches, holes, tears, punctures or other damage, do not use that pair.

Put your eclipse glasses on before looking towards the Sun and turn away from the Sun before removing them. Children should be supervised to make sure the glasses remain correctly positioned while they are looking upwards.

There is another important distinction: eclipse glasses are intended for unaided viewing with your eyes. They should not be used to look through binoculars, telescopes or camera lenses. Optical equipment concentrates sunlight and requires correctly fitted specialist solar filters designed for that equipment.

WHAT IF YOU CAN'T GET GLASSES IN TIME?

You can still experience the eclipse without looking directly at the Sun. A simple pinhole projector allows sunlight to pass through a small opening and project an image of the partially eclipsed Sun onto another surface.

Whatever method you choose, do not improvise with ordinary sunglasses, tinted glass or homemade eye filters.

WHEN CAN ROCHDALE SEE IT?

The eclipse takes place on Wednesday 12 August, beginning in the early evening and reaching maximum coverage shortly after 7pm in the Greater Manchester area. Around nine-tenths of the Sun is expected to be obscured at maximum, weather permitting.

It should create an extraordinary sight across Rochdale - but the most important preparation is making sure everyone watching has suitable eye protection before looking towards the Sun.

articles.title: Norden residents report being without water since Friday morning as outage continues
articles.excerpt: Residents in Norden say they have been without water since around 9am on Friday, with households reporting an extended loss of supply and frustration over the apparent lack of an on-site response.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Norden are reporting that they have been without running water since around 9am on Friday, with the disruption continuing into Saturday and households asking when their supply will return.

Rochdale Daily has received reports from residents describing a prolonged loss of supply and saying they have seen no sign of United Utilities teams in their immediate area. At the time of publication, Rochdale Daily has not independently confirmed the cause, the precise number of properties affected or an estimated restoration time.

The length of the reported interruption is significant. United Utilities' published standards say that where a burst on one of its pipes causes an unexpected loss of supply, it aims to restore water within 12 hours. The company says that where it identifies that it has failed to restore supply within 12 hours, household customers should automatically receive £50, plus another £50 for each additional 12-hour period they remain without water. Eligibility will depend on the circumstances of the interruption and the company's standards.

WHAT SHOULD RESIDENTS DO?

Anyone still without water should report the problem directly to United Utilities, even if neighbours have already done so. Its 24-hour water and wastewater number is 0345 672 3723. Residents can also use the United Utilities website to check for active incidents affecting their postcode and report water-supply problems.

If neighbouring properties have water but yours does not, United Utilities advises carrying out basic household checks. The internal stop tap, commonly located beneath the kitchen sink, can be turned off and back on several times while the cold kitchen tap is running, which may clear an airlock or obstruction. If an entire street or neighbourhood is affected, the problem is more likely to be on the wider network and should be reported to the company.

Residents should keep a record of when their supply stopped, any reference numbers given by United Utilities, screenshots of incident updates and details of calls or messages. This may be useful if the interruption later qualifies for a standards-of-service payment or if a complaint needs to be escalated.

VULNERABLE RESIDENTS AND BOTTLED WATER

People who are older, disabled, have medical needs, mobility difficulties, young children at home or otherwise need additional support should tell United Utilities immediately and ask about its free Priority Services scheme.

United Utilities says that if water is likely to remain off for more than 12 hours it will try to make alternative supplies available in the affected area. Priority Services customers who cannot collect alternative supplies may be able to receive bottled water at home.

Priority Services can be contacted on 0345 072 6093. United Utilities' published Priority Services commitments also include bottled-water support during qualifying prolonged emergency interruptions, with enhanced arrangements for its most vulnerable customers.

Residents who rely on water for home dialysis or another essential medical treatment should make this clear when contacting the company rather than waiting for a general area update.

If United Utilities confirms an alternative bottled-water collection point, Rochdale Daily will add the location to this story.

WHAT ABOUT COMPENSATION?

United Utilities' current standards of service state that an unexpected mains interruption lasting beyond 12 hours can trigger an automatic £50 payment, followed by a further £50 for each additional 12-hour period without water where the relevant standard applies. Residents should therefore retain evidence of the duration of the outage and check subsequent bills or correspondence.

If an eligible payment is not made, customers can raise the matter directly with United Utilities through its complaints process.

articles.title: Are our reservoirs recovering after Rochdale's exceptionally dry summer?
articles.excerpt: North West reservoir stocks fell sharply during July, but the latest verified figures show the region entered the dry spell with considerably more water in storage than at the same point last year.
articles.content_html:
After weeks of heat, dry ground and remarkably little rainfall, attention is turning to the North West's reservoirs — and whether the return of more changeable weather has begun to undo the damage.

The short answer is: not yet, based on the latest reservoir figures Rochdale Daily has been able to verify — although the overall regional position remains considerably better than it was this time last year.

United Utilities publishes figures covering the major reservoir systems supplying the North West. For the week ending 19 July, total regional reservoir storage stood at 70.6%. That was down 4.1 percentage points in just one week and slightly below the 72.7% average for that point in the year.

Of particular interest to Rochdale are United Utilities' Pennine sources. These were at 64.3% capacity by 19 July, having fallen four percentage points in a week. The normal level for that point in the year is 66.6%.

There is some reassuring context. At the same point last year, the Pennine sources were at just 42.2%. That means that despite this summer's prolonged dry weather, Pennine storage remained more than 20 percentage points higher than during the equivalent week of 2025.

Haweswater and Thirlmere — enormously important components of the North West's water-supply system — stood at a combined 67%. That represented a fall of 4.7 percentage points in a week, although it remained above the 64% seasonal average and above last year's 60.3%. At Thirlmere itself, the water surface was recorded at 4.01 metres below top water level.

Across the major reservoir groups, regional storage was 70.6%, Pennine sources 64.3%, Haweswater and Thirlmere 67%, Dee and Vyrnwy 76.5%, and Carlisle 66.8%. Every major group recorded a weekly decline, with Carlisle falling nine percentage points in a week.

So will a few rainy days refill them? Unfortunately, reservoirs do not work quite that quickly. Rain falling onto Rochdale does not translate immediately into an equivalent rise in reservoir storage. After a prolonged dry spell, rainfall must interact with dry soils, vegetation, rivers and the wider catchment before significant quantities reach reservoirs, while homes and businesses continue using water every day.

This is why several genuinely wet periods — rather than a couple of showers — can be required before reservoir levels show a meaningful and sustained recovery. The North West also operates as an interconnected water-supply system, meaning Rochdale's water security cannot be judged simply by looking at the nearest reservoir and seeing how full it appears.

The dry conditions have accompanied an exceptionally hot start to summer. By the middle of July, England and Wales had each received only around 34% of their normal rainfall for the entire summer season, despite being halfway through meteorological summer. Some locations had recorded no measurable July rainfall at all by that point.

Temperatures have also been extraordinary. By 15 July, the UK had already experienced more days above 30C during 2026 than occurred during the whole of the famously hot summer of 1976.

The Environment Agency has consequently been closely monitoring water resources across England, while United Utilities was under enhanced monitoring and operations for its Haweswater and Carlisle water-resource zones during July. Wildfires across Greater Manchester, Cheshire and Derbyshire created additional pressure, with significant quantities of water also required for firefighting.

The figures require perspective. Storage has fallen substantially and the Pennine system was below its seasonal average in the latest verified snapshot, but this is not the same situation as last summer. Pennine sources being at 64.3% compared with 42.2% at the same point in 2025 gives the region considerably more resilience. Haweswater and Thirlmere were also above both their seasonal average and last year's level.

The key question now is what happens during August. Several weeks of regular rainfall could begin rebuilding water resources. A return to prolonged heat and dry weather, however, would place further pressure on reservoir stocks at precisely the time when summer water demand remains high.

For Rochdale residents looking at exposed reservoir banks and wondering whether recent rain means the problem is over, the answer is more complicated: the North West entered the dry spell with a healthier reserve than last year, but reservoir stocks have been falling quickly and recovery requires sustained rainfall rather than the occasional wet day.

Rochdale Daily will continue tracking reservoir levels as new figures are published.

articles.title: Rare partial solar eclipse will be visible over Rochdale on Wednesday
articles.excerpt: A major partial solar eclipse will be visible across the UK on Wednesday 12 August, with around nine-tenths of the Sun expected to be obscured from the Rochdale area if skies remain clear.
articles.content_html:
People across Rochdale will have the chance to see one of the most striking astronomical events visible from the UK in years when a partial solar eclipse takes place on Wednesday 12 August.

The Met Office says the extent of the Sun's coverage and the precise timing of maximum obscuration will vary across the country, while local cloud and weather conditions will determine how much people are actually able to see.

Across the UK the eclipse will be substantial. Northeast Scotland is expected to see around 88 per cent of the Sun covered shortly before 7pm, while the far southwest of England will see around 96 per cent coverage shortly after 7.15pm.

For Greater Manchester and Rochdale, the eclipse is expected to begin at around 6.13pm, reach maximum obscuration at approximately 7.10pm and finish shortly after 8pm. Around 90 per cent of the Sun is expected to be covered at maximum, although the exact figure varies slightly by location.

The Royal Observatory Greenwich says the 12 August eclipse will be the largest partial solar eclipse visible from the UK and Ireland since 1999.

WEATHER COULD MAKE OR BREAK THE VIEW

Even a major eclipse can disappear behind typical British cloud, so anyone hoping to watch it should check the latest local forecast on the day. Thin or broken cloud may still allow glimpses, while thicker cloud could block the event completely.

HOW TO WATCH SAFELY

The Met Office stresses that people must never look directly at the Sun. Ordinary sunglasses are not safe for viewing an eclipse.

Certified eclipse glasses designed specifically for direct solar viewing can be used if they are undamaged and meet the appropriate safety standard. Another safe option is a pinhole projector, which allows the Sun's image to be projected onto a surface without looking directly at it.

Cameras, binoculars and telescopes should never be pointed at the Sun unless they are fitted with specialist solar filters designed for the equipment. Looking through an optical device without suitable protection can cause severe and permanent eye injury.

For residents lucky enough to get clear skies, Wednesday evening should provide a rare opportunity to see daylight noticeably dim as the Moon passes across most of the Sun's disc.

Rochdale Daily will monitor the local forecast ahead of the eclipse and update readers if viewing conditions become clearer.

articles.title: Comment: Rochdale Canal should be the jewel in the town's crown
articles.excerpt: Steven Parker of the Rochdale Canal Group argues that a living canal basin filled with boats, heritage, independent businesses and public space could bring visitors, jobs and regeneration to Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
This is a comment article by Steven Parker of the Rochdale Canal Group. The views expressed are his own.

Rochdale Branch Canal

Industrial units will not bring visitors to Rochdale, but a living canal basin filled with boats, a heritage centre, café, independent shops and exhibition space most definitely will.

Our historic canals should be the jewel in Rochdale's crown, but instead they languish neglected and forgotten.

The time is right for real change along the Rochdale Canal corridor, and we must be instrumental in making it happen.

A revitalised canal corridor has the potential to offer far more than an attractive waterside environment. Done properly, regeneration could create environmental improvements, attract visitors, support independent businesses, create employment and reconnect Rochdale with an extraordinary part of its industrial heritage.

A living canal basin would give people a reason to spend time in Rochdale rather than simply pass through it. Boats bring movement and activity. A heritage centre could tell the story of the canal and the industries it once served. Cafés, independent shops and exhibition spaces could provide places for residents and visitors to meet, spend money and experience something distinctive to the town.

Rochdale's industrial history should not simply be something remembered in photographs. The surviving canal corridor provides an opportunity to use that history as part of the borough's future.

Environmental, regenerative and job-creation opportunities will follow if Rochdale is ambitious enough to recognise the potential sitting alongside its historic waterways.

The opportunity is there. The question is whether Rochdale is prepared to take it.

Steven Parker Rochdale Canal Group Originally written 8 September 2024.

articles.title: Prehistoric survivor growing in Syke herb garden has roots stretching back 300 million years
articles.excerpt: Residents picking herbs from a community garden in Syke are being invited to help tackle horsetail — a persistent weed whose ancestors grew locally more than 300 million years ago.
articles.content_html:
A troublesome weed growing in a community herb garden in Syke has a remarkable connection to the landscape's prehistoric past — with its ancestors dating back more than 300 million years.

Residents are being encouraged to help maintain the community herb garden while collecting fresh herbs to take home.

The garden is open for people to pick herbs for their own use, but volunteers are asking visitors who have a few spare minutes to lend a hand with some weeding at the same time.

One plant in particular is proving difficult to control: horsetail, also commonly known as mare's tail.

While modern gardeners may regard it as a persistent nuisance, horsetail belongs to an extraordinarily ancient group of plants whose history stretches back to long before dinosaurs walked the Earth.

During the Carboniferous period, more than 300 million years ago, relatives of today's horsetails grew across the landscapes that would eventually become northern England.

Among them were Calamites — tree-like plants related to modern horsetails which could grow many metres tall and formed part of the vast Carboniferous vegetation.

Evidence of that lost landscape can still be found locally. A fossil discovered in a quarry at Tonacliffe shows the distinctive remains of Calamites, providing a physical connection between the plants growing here hundreds of millions of years ago and the much smaller horsetails residents battle in gardens today.

Carboniferous plant fossils can also be found within rocks across the surrounding moorland, reflecting a period when the area's environment looked dramatically different from the Pennine landscape residents know today.

People remain welcome to collect herbs from the community garden, but anyone visiting is being encouraged to pull a few weeds while they are there.

As the volunteers joked, nobody wants today's horsetail growing to the size of its Carboniferous grandparents.

The community garden is maintained for local people to enjoy, and even a few minutes of weeding can help keep it productive and accessible for everyone.

articles.title: Plans for 45 homes behind Greenvale unanimously deferred after more than 290 objections
articles.excerpt: Councillors have unanimously deferred a planning application for 45 homes on land behind Greenvale in Bamford after campaigners raised concerns over transport, drainage, biodiversity, design and the absence of a wider masterplan.
articles.content_html:
A controversial planning application for 45 homes on land behind Greenvale in Bamford has been unanimously deferred after a packed Planning Committee meeting and more than 290 public objections.

The application had been recommended for approval by planning officers, but strong public interest saw it moved to the first item on the committee agenda.

Claire, chair of Bamford Green Belt Action Group, Dr Barry Lewis and Councillor Steve Anstee addressed the committee, asking councillors either to refuse the proposal or defer a decision while outstanding issues were examined further.

Campaigners raised a wide range of concerns, including the absence of a comprehensive masterplan for the wider allocation of around 450 homes and the lack of an infrastructure phasing and delivery strategy.

Transport was another major issue. Objectors highlighted Transport for Greater Manchester's position that effective transport mitigation could not yet be determined, while concerns were also raised over the proposed access through Greenvale and Norford Way rather than Norden Road.

Existing drainage and pedestrian-safety problems were raised during the meeting. Dr Lewis highlighted drainage issues already experienced on Norford Way and also questioned proposals relating to affordable and social housing beneath power lines.

Environmental concerns included a reported 39 per cent biodiversity net loss, rather than the 10 per cent biodiversity net gain required under current rules. Campaigners also pointed to outstanding concerns from ecology and urban-design officers.

United Utilities was said to have requested an allocation-wide drainage masterplan, while further concerns were raised about design, affordable housing, recreational facilities and the absence of what campaigners considered appropriate pre-application public consultation.

More than 290 objections have been submitted by members of the public.

Following debate, councillors voted unanimously to defer the application until September to allow further work and clarification.

The decision does not amount to a refusal of the proposed development. The application remains live and is expected to return to councillors once the outstanding matters have been considered.

Bamford Green Belt Action Group described the deferral as an important result and thanked residents who attended the meeting, submitted objections or supported the campaign.

Rochdale Daily will report further developments when the application returns to the Planning Committee.
